title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Outline


The importance of people for public service
What is human resource management (HRM)?
Basic components of HRM in government and nonprofit organizations
Thinking about HRM in government and nonprofit organizations



Or why we have a separate course on this and do not just send you to the business school.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Running Government and Nonprofit Organizations

Four main types of resources:



Human


Financial


Information


Time



Without motivated people, the rest of these resources will be squandered.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
The Importance of People

Human resources are critical to organizational performance in government and nonprofit organizations
In government —

People are the hands and feet of government, bringing policy to life

In nonprofits —

People have the opportunity to tailor their public service to different communities of people to try to make a difference

When people work in public service, they have expectations for that employment relationship


HRM is the aspect of management that accentuates and guides the human processes involved in the pursuit of public purposes.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
What is Human Resource Management?

Word association: when I say “human resource management” or “personnel administration,” what comes to mind? Have the students list and explain terms, list them on the board, and discuss. Use this discussion to transition to the next slide.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
The Scope of HRM

It encompasses many different functions:



Job design


Hiring and firing


Compensation and benefits


Training and development


Performance appraisal


Labor-management relations


Work-life balance issues



Highlight how many of the classes over the course of the semester will involve deeper dives into these different functions.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Human Capital

Effective HRM is about building a strong complement of human capital and using it well
What is human capital?

Human capital brought to an organization makes the difference between success and failure

Human capital is critical for organizational performance
To harness the power of human capital, HR managers must be part of the strategic direction-setting of the organization


This term captures what people bring to organizations; it is the value they add. It includes all their knowledge, skills, abilities, and competencies.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service

THE STRATEGIC VIEW: how does managing people connect to organizational performance? Adapted from OPM’s Human Capital Assessment and Accountability Framework (HCAAF). Read as the management cycle: strategic alignment (HR tied to mission) provides direction → leadership & knowledge management, results-oriented performance culture, and talent management deliver outcomes → accountability measures results. Key feature is the feedback loop: performance information flows back into planning — a learning organization. Punchline: HR belongs in the room where strategy is set. Previews next week’s strategic HRM class.
HRM is about aligning human capital with the goals of the organization to achieve them and produce high performance. Also emphasize it is about building a learning organization where results are evaluated and used to make continuous improvements over time.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
The System of HRM Functions


  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    • Position management
    • Compensation & benefits
    • Legal rights & responsibilities
    • Labor relations & collective
    bargaining
    
    standardizing
  
  
    
    
    • Recruitment
    • Selection
    • Training & development
    • Grievance process
    • Employee-friendly policies
    
    humanizing
  
  
    
    
    • Performance appraisal
    • Employee surveys
    • System performance
    
    evaluating
  



THE OPERATIONAL VIEW: sorts HRM’s everyday toolbox by the purpose each function serves. Standardizing = fairness through consistency (same rules for everyone). Humanizing = fairness through responsiveness (employees as individuals). Evaluating = feedback on both. Key tension: standardizing vs. humanizing — a good system holds them in balance. Contrast with the previous figure: that one looks up and out (HRM → organizational performance); this one looks inward (what HRM does day to day). Also a roadmap of the semester — most weeks deep-dive one box.
Emphasize how HRM fits together HR functions in a system that ensures people are treated fairly, but their particular needs and differences are recognized (humanizing). The system also evaluates the functions and uses that information to make continuous improvements. This sets up the manager vs. employee activity on the next slide.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Activity: Manager vs. Employee

Which category matters most — standardizing, humanizing, or evaluating?


Left side of the room: you are the HR manager. Right side: you are the employee.
In groups of 3–4, rank the three categories from your assigned perspective — and be ready to defend your #1. (8 minutes)
Each group reports its ranking; then we debate across the aisle.


Where do the two perspectives collide — and what tensions does that create for how HRM is designed?


Keep the System of HRM Functions figure available to flip back to. Expect managers to lean standardizing/evaluating (fairness, defensibility, performance) and employees to lean humanizing (recognition, development, grievances). Push on the collisions: standardizing protects equity but can feel dehumanizing; evaluating drives improvement but can feel like surveillance. Land on the point that a good HRM system holds all three in tension — none is dispensable. Roughly 20–25 minutes total: 8 in groups, then report-outs and cross-room debate.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
The Scope of HRM — Part 2

HRM is governed by laws:

Some of which have endured for generations
Some of which are modified by ever-evolving case law

How do we make sense of this complex array of venues, practices, policies, and legal requirements?
We do so by focusing on:

The people involved
How these processes work
The ways in which people and processes combine to achieve the mission

text: Private Sector and Public Service HRM… What’s the difference?

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Public Service HRM

Expectations of the public service workforce are many

Both performance standards and democratic standards

Beyond job skills, public servants are expected to embody public integrity and to perform their jobs from a position of partisan neutrality
They are expected to be representative of the constituencies served
Their actions are subject to public scrutiny
Processes imposed on these workers are designed to ensure fairness, organizational justice, and equity

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
section: Exercise: What does it mean to be a public servant?
text:
Exercise: What does it mean to be a public servant?

What should the expectations be? Obligations?


What does this mean for managing people in public organizations?

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text: Comparing Government and Nonprofit HRM

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Government vs. Nonprofit: Similarities

Functions of HRM are mostly the same across government and nonprofit organizations
Both government and nonprofits need to think about values and accountability…
BUT — context matters:

Laws
Systems
Capacity

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Government vs. Nonprofit: Differences

Civil service systems: advantages and disadvantages?
Politics: How does partisan politics influence HRM in government?
Capacity: How does capacity influence differences between government and nonprofit organizations?


Civil service systems: government often has more formalized HRM systems that require balancing stability with innovation and change. Many government employees have employment protections by law. Nonprofits do not have civil service systems and can be more agile — but employees have fewer protections compared to government. Politics: how does partisan politics influence HRM in government? In nonprofits, less of an issue. Capacity: how does capacity influence differences between government and nonprofit organizations?

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
section: The Role of Merit in HRM
text: The Role of Merit in HRM

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Merit Principles

Codified in federal law
Merit principles were created for government employment; they attempt to capture principles of effective, equitable, and fair HRM
…so should be applicable to other types of organizations

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
The Merit Principles

Codified in federal law



1Employee selection is based on knowledge, skills, and ability through fair and open competition.


2Job applicants and employees must be treated equitably with proper regard for their privacy and constitutional rights.


3Employees must receive equal pay for work of equal value.


4High standards of conduct are expected and concern for the public interest is foremost.


5The workforce is to be guided by norms of efficiency and effectiveness.


6Employees are to be retained based on their performance; inadequate performance is to be dealt with fairly and decisively.


7Training of employees should focus on both individual and organizational performance.


8Employees are to be protected from favoritism, political coercion, and arbitrary actions.


9Employees are to be protected against reprisal for whistleblowing.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
section: Activity: Merit Principles in the Wild
text:
Activity: Merit Principles in the Wild

Take the nine principles from paper to practice — in groups of 3–4:


Honored: pick one principle you have seen genuinely upheld in a workplace. What made it work?
Violated: pick one you have seen violated (no names needed). What happened, and what did it cost?
Missing: is anything missing from the list? Would you add — or cut — a principle?

(10 minutes in groups, then each group shares one story or proposal.)

These were written for government — how well do they travel to nonprofits, or to the private sector?


Flip back to the Merit Principles slide while groups work, or hand out a printed list. Groups of 3–4 gives four or five groups at current enrollment. In the debrief, take one item per group so everyone speaks; violations usually produce the richest discussion — press on what the violation cost the organization (turnover, morale, trust). The “missing/cut” question surfaces whether students think the principles are aspirational or enforceable. Close by previewing that Chapter 3 digs into merit systems in depth, so tonight is about intuitions, not doctrine. Roughly 20–25 minutes total.

title: Introduction to HR in Public Service
text:
Bringing it all together…

People are critical for government and nonprofit organizations in working toward organizational missions
Skillful management maximizes human capital
HRM is a system, involving many functions that promote different values and purposes
HRM is different in public service — government and nonprofit employees hold a public trust and need to be cognizant of what this means

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Tonight’s questions

How do people and HR practices help an organization accomplish its mission?


Strategic alignment, workforce planning, and succession planning


Sources throughout: Mary E. Guy and Jessica E. Sowa, Human Resource Essentials for Public Service: People, Process, Performance (2022), Chapter 2 author slides and instructor manual, Chapter 2, pp. 17–24. This opening adapts author slides 1–2. Examples marked hypothetical are classroom applications, not reported findings.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
A workforce challenge

Think of a government or nonprofit organization you know. What workforce problem makes its mission harder to achieve?


What work suffers?
What would a manager need to know before responding?


Five minutes in groups. Put it on the white board.


Write each group’s problem on the board under “Tonight’s problems” and leave it up. Reuse them on the alignment, gaps-and-surpluses, succession, and measures slides, and in the closing activity. Define a workforce challenge or give an example if the room stalls. Connect to Chapter 1: human capital includes knowledge, skills, abilities, and competencies. About six minutes including the round.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Strategic human resource management
HR decisions connect the organization’s people and capabilities to its goals.

What does the organization need to accomplish?
What capabilities will that require?
How will HR practices develop and support those capabilities?
What evidence will show whether the approach works?


People are an asset to develop, not a cost to minimize. Strategic HRM moves from managing positions to managing talent.


Source: author slides 5 and 7; instructor manual p. 17. Strategic HRM is an ongoing approach to managing people. Workforce planning is one way to put that approach into practice. Plant the takeaway line now: Urbanopolis after the break is a budget process that treats people as a cost line. Ask students to watch for where Pat can still act as if people are the asset.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
HR’s role in organizational decisions


Transactional
Accurate pay, benefits, records, and dependable employment processes


Transformational
A seat at the table: advice about staffing capacity, employee development, and whether organizational goals are feasible



Strategic HRM depends on reliable administration and a voice in setting direction.


Where you work: is HR asked before a commitment is made, or after?


Source: author slide 7 and its notes, instructor manual p. 17 (transactional and transformational components). Take two or three answers to the question on the slide; ask what happened when HR came in after the commitment. Avoid treating transactional work as unimportant.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Alignment across management systems


  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Organizational
    goal
  
  
    
    Strategic planning
    What result are we trying to achieve?
    
  
  
    
    Budgeting
    What resources can sustain the work?
    
  
  
    
    Human resource management
    Who can do the work, and what support do they need?
    
  
  
    
    Information technology
    What tools and information will staff use?
    
  



The arrows run both ways. Are any of these systems missing from where you work?


Sources: author slides 8–9, recreating the alignment SmartArt (organizational goals at the hub; HRM, budgeting, strategic planning, IT around it). The questions are teaching applications. Build the hub one system at a time. Emphasize mutual adjustment: workforce capacity can reshape strategy as well as respond to it. Point at a problem on the board and ask which system created it or could fix it.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
section: A service goal with conflicting incentives
text:
A service goal with conflicting incentives

Hypothetical: a benefits office
The office wants residents to receive accurate eligibility decisions sooner.
Managers reward staff for closing more cases each day. Training time reduces that daily count.


What behavior does this system encourage?


Instructor-created hypothetical applying author slide 9. Ask whether speed alone captures the mission. Probe for errors, repeat contacts, appeals, staff learning, and access. Do not supply an answer before students diagnose the mismatch.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Performance and public service values


  
    
      
    
  
  
    
    Capacity
    building
    
    Talent
    development
    
    Performance
    
    Metrics
    
    
    
    EVIDENCE-BASED HRM PRACTICE
  
  
    
    Organizational justice
    
    Public service values
    
    Diversity and inclusion
    
    Representative bureaucracy
    
    
    
    
  



Whose experience disappears when we report only an average processing time?


Source: author slide 6, recreating its cycle-matrix SmartArt: four wedges of practice (capacity building, talent development, performance, metrics) cycling around a center, each with the value the author places beside it: organizational justice by capacity building, public service values by talent development, diversity and inclusion by performance, representative bureaucracy by metrics. First reveal: the practice cycle, an evidence-based approach of gathering workforce data and using it to build capacity and develop talent. Second reveal: the values environment; the author’s notes ask students to consider how each value shapes the neighboring practice. Connect to Chapter 1’s discussion of merit and public service. Take answers to the question on the slide; the choice of a performance measure is itself a judgment about what matters.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
section: What a strategic approach can offer
text:
What a strategic approach can offer


For employees
A clearer connection between their work and the mission, useful feedback, and support for development


For managers
Evidence for resource decisions and a way to assess whether new commitments fit existing capacity



Strategy also means knowing what not to do. Would an attractive new grant make the organization less able to deliver what it already promises?


Source: author slide 10 and its notes (Porter on strategy as knowing what not to do). These are potential benefits, not guaranteed effects. Introduce mission creep as taking on work that diverts capacity from core purposes; the takeaway question is the manual’s grant example.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Workforce planning

Source: author slide 11. Transition from the strategic approach to a concrete planning process.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
The workforce planning process

Five steps, cyclical



1 · Direction

What must we accomplish?



→


2 · Analysis

What workforce do we have, and what do we need?



→


3 · Action plan

How will we close the gaps?



→


4 · Implement

Who is responsible for each action, by when?



→


5 · Evaluate

Did it work? What needs revising?




Discovering a workforce constraint may send you back to the goal, the budget, or the timeline.


Source: author slide 12. Present this as an iterative process. The strip at the top of the next slides shows where we are in it.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
section: Strategic direction and the HR audit
text:
Strategic direction and the HR audit

1 Direction2 Analysis3 Action plan4 Implement5 Evaluate

Direction: What must the organization accomplish now and over the next several years?
HR audit: What do existing policies, practices, and workforce information reveal about its ability to do that work?

Review roles, staffing, compensation, and performance processes.
Identify what works and where capacity or information is missing.


Source: author slide 13 and instructor manual p. 18. Explain that an HR audit is a structured assessment, not simply an employee count. It can expose outdated job descriptions, inconsistent practices, or missing information. No legal compliance determination is being made here.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
section: Activity: the staffing implications of a goal
text:
Activity: the staffing implications of a goal

Hypothetical: a city will open its permit counter two evenings each week using its existing staffing budget.


What work and skills will evening service require?
What do you need to learn about the current workforce?
Are there any tradeoffs leadership resolve should before promising this service?

Think about the potential varying perspectives : HR director · budget analyst · counter supervisor · resident who works days

Five minutes in groups.


Instructor-created hypothetical adapting author slide 14’s strategic-goal exercise. Assign one role per group (four groups of three). Allow about eight minutes including reports. The roles should produce disagreement: HR sees training and supervision; Budget sees the flat budget; the supervisor sees daytime coverage and burnout; the resident sees access. Listen for scheduling, supervision, IT support, training, workload, and effects on daytime service. Keep the focus on translating a goal into workforce requirements.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
section: The workforce we have and the workforce we need
text:
The workforce we have and the workforce we need

1 Direction2 Analysis3 Action plan4 Implement5 Evaluate









Current workforce
Future requirements




Knowledge, Skills, Abilities
Work needed to meet service goals


Career stage and anticipated departures
Capabilities that may disappear


Hours, positions, and funding sources
Sustainable staffing and funding


Current workload and constraints
Gaps, surpluses, or work to redesign


Rules, contracts, and required staffing levels
Constraints any plan must respect





Source: author slide 15, including its line on external constraints or rules (accreditation, safety staffing). The constraints row sets up Urbanopolis: budget instructions that allow only supervisory cuts, deleted classifications, and pending union negotiations. Distinguish headcount, funded positions, and full-time equivalents. Two half-time employees can equal one FTE. Avoid treating demographic categories as proxies for an individual’s abilities or retirement plans. Gather evidence about actual skills and likely departures.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Responses to gaps and surpluses

1 Direction2 Analysis3 Action plan4 Implement5 Evaluate



A capability gap
Recruit, develop current employees, redesign work, or reconsider the service commitment.


A surplus in some work
Consider redeployment, retraining, attrition, or position reductions in light of service needs.



An organization can have a surplus in one role/position and a shortage in another.


Sources: author slide 16, instructor manual p. 20 workforce-planning definition and discussion of gaps and surpluses. Options here are illustrative and depend on authority, rules, costs, and timing. Ask students to return to the permit-counter example, or a problem on the board: what could they do immediately, and what would require time or approval?

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Succession planning

1 Direction2 Analysis3 Action plan4 Implement5 Evaluate

Which departures would put essential work at risk?

Identify key leadership and service positions.
Identify the competencies future employees will need.
Develop internal capability and consider external recruitment.
Prepare for an unexpected vacancy as well as a planned transition.


Sources: author slides 17–19 and instructor manual p. 20. A critical position can be a specialist or frontline role. Succession planning includes knowledge transfer and development. It should not imply a guaranteed promotion for a chosen successor. Ask whether any problem on the board is really a succession problem.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
section: A vacancy beyond the leadership team
text:
A vacancy beyond the leadership team

Hypothetical: one experienced analyst
Only one analyst knows how to produce a required monthly report. The report draws on several systems, and the process lives mostly in the analyst’s memory.


Show of hands: are you the only person at work who knows how to do something?


What should the manager do before that person leaves?


Instructor-created hypothetical applying author slides 18–19. Take the show of hands first; ask one or two people what the thing is and what happens when they take a week off. Then the question. Listen for documentation, cross-training, protected learning time, and backup responsibility. Probe: who has time to learn? How would you know the backup can actually complete the work? Keep to roughly three minutes.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Implementation and accountability
A workforce plan needs an owner, resources, and a timeline.

Assign responsibility for each action.
Agree on measures and review dates.
Discuss progress in regular management meetings.
Adjust when results or service needs change.


Source: author slide 20, including the implementation SmartArt. Emphasize feasibility: a training plan without time for employees to attend is incomplete.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Measures that help managers learn








Management question
Possible evidence




Can we fill needed roles?
Vacancy duration and qualified applicant pools


Can staff perform the work?
Demonstrated competencies and error rates


Is service improving?
Timeliness, accuracy, and differences across users


Can we sustain the improvement?
Turnover, workload, and employee feedback





Instructor-created examples applying author slides 6, 9, and 20. Measures describe possible evidence, not established causal relationships. Ask what comparison or baseline would be useful. If errors rise, consider changes in case complexity or systems alongside workforce explanations.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
section: What would you tell your manager?
text:
What would you tell your manager?

Return to the workforce problem your group put on the board.


What organizational goal is at stake?
What evidence would you gather first?
What HR decision might that evidence change?


Sources: author slides 21–22 and instructor manual pp. 20–21. Leave roughly four minutes. Ask for one changed answer from the opening discussion. Reinforce the link between the mission, workforce capabilities, and evidence.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Urbanopolis after the break

Transition to the separate Urbanopolis deck. Students read the case excerpt, pages 1–9. Source: Brett S. Sharp, Budget Reorganization in the Urbanopolis Human Resources Department (Electronic Hallway, 2008). Instructor manual p. 21 recommends the case to consider strategic HRM under fiscal constraint.

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
Pat Alvarez’s decision
You are the new HR director in a growing city of more than one million residents.
You must propose a smaller HR budget and a reorganization while developing the city’s reduction-in-force policy.

How should HR preserve the capacity to serve the city under these constraints?

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
The budget target




Current budget
Proposed budget
Required reduction




$2,698,150
$2,468,807
$229,343





An 8.5% cut in a budget that is about 97% salaries and benefits.
Average salary about $35,000; benefits a flat $4,500 per employee.
New computers must come from labor savings. Surplus police computers are the temporary alternative.
The vacant Risk Manager is one of the 65 funded positions. Filling it uses the vacancy savings that now pay an overage employee (p. 6).
Recruitment advertising is already overspent this year (p. 5). Council wants a nationwide search.

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
The rules and competing demands

Cuts may fall only on supervisory positions.
Six classifications disappear from the management pay plan on July 1: Assistant Director, Administrative Assistant, Secretary III, Administrative Officer, Operations Support Manager, Planner.
The Council wants the vacant Risk Manager position filled through a nationwide search.
65 budgeted positions, eight regular vacancies, and seven filled overage positions.
Union negotiations are coming, and HR must write the citywide RIF policy before the budget is final.

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
section: What problem should Pat solve first?
text:
What problem should Pat solve first?

What is your first move as Pat, and why?

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
section: What must the city still be able to do?
text:
What must the city still be able to do?

What work must HR still perform while the department gets smaller?


Even with fewer staff, the city must still:

Fill critical vacancies
Pay employees and administer benefits accurately
Manage labor relations and the reduction in force
Review job classifications and departmental reorganizations
Maintain personnel records and legal compliance
Train or reassign employees as responsibilities change



Which two capabilities would you protect first? What evidence would justify those priorities?

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
Fewer layers of supervision
Budget’s premise: the average department has four layers of management between first-line workers and the department head, and that is redundant.

When would removing a supervisory layer improve service? When could it make service worse?

What would you need to know before deciding that a layer is redundant?

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
A recommendation for city management

In groups of 3–4, develop a provisional approach to the reorganization.


Identify one capability to protect and one change to investigate.
Which budget instruction is hardest for your approach to satisfy? What would you need to know to satisfy it?
Name the most serious service or employee consequence.
Identify the missing evidence that could change your recommendation.

Approaches on the table: remove a layer, consolidate supervision, reclassify into allowed titles, or make the case to the Assistant City Managers for a softer target (p. 6). If you negotiate, say what evidence you bring.

Eight minutes. Use the handout’s chart and pay bands to inform your decisions.

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
Which recommendation holds up?

What is the strongest objection to the approach you prefer?

Which assumption makes the recommendation work, and what happens if it is wrong?

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
section: Rules that apply to HR itself
text:
Rules that apply to HR itself

What should make a citywide reduction-in-force policy fair and credible?

How should Pat weigh service needs, performance, and seniority?
Is a reduction in force an occasion for participatory management, or does it require a top-down approach?

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
The assistant director
The City Manager praises Alexandar Vineta’s experience and loyalty.
Assistant Director is also one of the classifications the budget instructions eliminate.

What should Pat do with these two messages?


The City Manager who praised Vineta also approves every reorganization (p. 7). One person sent both messages. The position costs about $72,000 loaded, roughly a third of the target.


New information for Pat: the Assistant Director is eligible for retirement and serves at the pleasure of the City Manager. Does that change your answer? Should it?

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
After the budget decision

Six months later, how would you know whether the reorganization worked?

What would you monitor besides spending, and what finding would make you change course?

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
Your recommendation now

What should Pat do next?

State your recommendation and the tradeoff you are willing to accept.

What changed in your thinking? What lesson would you carry into another organization?

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Tonight’s question

How do people and HR practices help an organization accomplish its mission?


Strategic alignment, workforce planning, and succession planning

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Implementation and evidence

1 Direction2 Analysis3 Action plan4 Implement5 Evaluate



A plan needs an owner, resources, and a timeline.

Assign responsibility for each action.
Agree on measures and review dates.
Discuss progress in regular management meetings.
Adjust when results or service needs change.










Management question
Possible evidence




Can we fill needed roles?
Vacancy duration, qualified applicant pools


Can staff perform the work?
Demonstrated competencies, error rates


Is service improving?
Timeliness, accuracy, differences across users


Can we sustain it?
Turnover, workload, employee feedback






Pick one problem from the board(s). What measure would provide evidence about whether it’s improving?


Sources: author slide 20, including the implementation SmartArt, and instructor-created measures applying author slides 6, 9, and 20. Emphasize feasibility: a training plan without time for employees to attend is incomplete. Measures describe possible evidence, not established causal relationships. Two minutes on the closing question: take one measure per group, and ask what comparison or baseline would be needed. If errors rise, consider changes in case complexity or systems alongside workforce explanations.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
text:
Two mindsets for strategic HRM


Growth
Hire, develop, and expand. Most of the chapter, and most of what the field teaches, assumes an organization that is adding capacity.


Austerity
Cut, consolidate, and reduce in force. The reality for many public and nonprofit organizations, and the harder test of whether people are treated as an asset.



Tonight’s case is strategic HRM under austerity. What can Pat Alvarez do?


Source: instructor manual p. 21, which recommends Urbanopolis because SHRM is usually taught “with a growth mindset” while most organizations face fiscal austerity. Say the line, then break. Pat has to cut 8.5% from a budget that is 97% people, write the citywide RIF rules, and fill a Council-priority vacancy at the same time.

title: Budget Reorganization in Urbanopolis
text:
What Urbanopolis HR actually does



Employment: recruitment, selection, test administration, reception
Occupational Health Clinic: physicals for Police and Fire recruits, workers’ comp, ADA accommodation
Administrative Finance: HRIS on a mainframe, records and the file room, Benefits, Job Training



Employee Relations: Classification, Labor Relations (three unions), Compensation
Workforce Development: federal grants, the metro “one-stop shop”
Human Rights / EEO: the annual Affirmative Action report
A secretarial pool and two executive secretaries

HR’s own chart



Count the layers between a Benefits Analyst and the Director.


Which of the six deleted classifications does HR actually hold?


Every employee has a PC. What is the secretarial pool for?



Source: full case p. 23, redrawn by title (no names, no demographic or performance data). Boxes: bold border = supervisory, gold = deleted classification, dashed = vacant, grey = overage, dotted = temporary. Same chart is page 3 of the handout. Benefits chain: Director, Assistant Director, Administrative Finance Manager, Benefits Manager, Benefits Supervisor, then the analysts. Four layers between a first-line worker and the department head, exactly Budget’s premise. The Compensation chain runs one deeper. Selected classifications on this chart: one Assistant Director, seven Administrative Assistants (three of them supervise a unit: reception and test administration, the file room, the secretarial pool; four are staff support), one Secretary III. None of Administrative Officer, Operations Support Manager, or Planner. So rule 3 is mostly a reclassification exercise into allowed titles such as Administrative Technician (grade 10) or Administrative Specialist (grade 13), not a layoff. Secretarial pool: one Administrative Assistant, three Secretary IIs, three temporary word processing operators. The temps are not among the 65 funded positions, so dispersing the pool saves little money by itself; the question is what the unit is for and where the supervisory position goes. Roughly twenty to twenty-five positions on the chart sit above someone. Vacancies: Risk Manager, two Senior HR Specialists (both supervisory), one HR Specialist, two Training Specialists, File Clerk, Receptionist.
